title_original: Ted Joans: The Art of Improvisation
excerpt_original: At the Musée cantonal des Beaux-Arts in Lausanne, Switzerland, curator Pierre-Henri Foulon revisits Ted Joans’ radical imagination through Ted Joans: Black Flower, exploring the intersections of jazz, Surrealism, Black identity, and Pan-Africanism. 26 November 2026 […]

blocks.text: At the Musée cantonal des Beaux-Arts in Lausanne, Switzerland, curator Pierre-Henri Foulon revisits Ted Joans’ radical imagination through Ted Joans: Black Flower , exploring the intersections of jazz, Surrealism, Black identity, and Pan-Africanism.

For Ted Joans (1928–2003), jazz was more than music, and Surrealism was more than an artistic movement. Both offered ways of thinking, creating and living outside established conventions. A poet, visual artist, performer and inveterate traveller, Joan moved between Africa, Europe and the United States, cultivating friendships and intellectual exchanges that informed his distinctive artistic language. His practice brought humour, improvisation and political conviction into dialogue with questions of Black identity, freedom and belonging. Despite his connections to some of the twentieth century’s most influential cultural movements, established art histories still insufficiently recognise his contribution.

In Ted Joans: Black Flower , the first monographic exhibition dedicated to his work, curator Pierre-Henri Foulon brings Joans’ creative practice into focus. In conversation with ART AFRICA , Foulon discusses the artist’s refusal of categorisation, his commitment to Black internationalism and the significance of reconsidering his legacy today. blocks.text: Suzette Bell-Roberts: Ted Joans: Black Flower is the first monographic exhibition dedicated to an artist whose practice crossed poetry, visual art, jazz and performance. What inspired you to revisit Joans’ legacy, and what did you discover through the exhibition’s research and development?

Pierre-Henri Foulon: What struck me was the gap between Joans’ extraordinary trajectory and his relative invisibility today. He appeared in countless histories of postwar culture, but usually in fragments, as a poet, a performer, a jazz enthusiast, a traveller, or a Surrealist. His visual work was never central to the discussion. Even people who knew him well often had little idea of the sheer scale and ambition of his artistic production. Researching the exhibition revealed an artist who moved seamlessly between words and images, and whose real medium was, in many ways, life itself. We aimed to bring that remarkable body of work into focus for the first time. Ted Joans, dans son studio d’Astor Place, avec en arrière-plan la peinture, Bird Lives! et quelques œuvres de la série Jazz Action, vers 1958. Tirage photographique, 20,3×25,2 cm. blocks.text: The exhibition takes its title from Joans’ 1968 poem and manifesto, Black Flower . How does this concept shape your curatorial approach, and what does it reveal about Joans’ understanding of Black identity, imagination and artistic freedom?

For Joans, the Black Flower symbolised creativity, resilience, and transformation. The expression emerged in the late 1960s, when he was closely engaged with the Black Power movement and reflecting on the political and cultural meanings of Blackness. The Black Flower expressed a vision of Black identity that was expansive rather than restrictive, rooted in history but open to constant reinvention. That idea shaped the exhibition from the outset. Rather than presenting a fixed portrait of the artist, we wanted to show a practice defined by openness, imagination, and freedom. It articulated a vision of Black identity that was expansive rather than restrictive, rooted in history yet open to constant reinvention. Collage, central to his creative approach, let seemingly disparate elements coexist, creating connections while preserving their differences. These ideas shaped the exhibition from the outset, informing the ways we brought together different aspects of his life and work. Rather than presenting a fixed portrait of the artist, we wanted to highlight a practice defined by openness. blocks.text: Joans moved between New York, Paris, Tangier and Timbuktu, developing an artistic practice shaped by encounters across continents. How did his relationship with Africa and its diaspora influence his creative vision, and how have you explored these connections in the exhibition?

Africa was transformative for Joan because it was a lived reality, not an abstract idea. From the 1960s onwards, he travelled extensively across the continent, and Timbuktu became one of the places he felt most attached to. He returned repeatedly and built lasting friendships there. At the same time, he became increasingly involved in Pan-African cultural networks, taking part in landmark gatherings such as the Pan- African Festival in Algiers and FESTAC in Lagos. For Joans, Africa was never simply a place of origin; it was a dynamic cultural and political space connecting Black communities worldwide. Many of the works in the exhibition emerged directly from these experiences, from poems and drawings to photographs and films. As he wrote, “Africa, you are in me / My future is your future / Your wounds are my wounds,” capturing a connection that was at once personal, political, and creative.

Jazz played a central role in Joans’ artistic philosophy, influencing not only his poetry but also his visual language and his approach to life. How have you incorporated the improvisational aspects of jazz into the structure and overall experience of the exhibition?

Joan often approached art the way a jazz musician approaches a performance. Improvisation, spontaneity, and collaboration were fundamental to his practice. Rather than imposing a strictly chronological narrative, we organised the exhibition around themes, echoes, and unexpected encounters. Visitors move between poetry, collage, film, and archival material much as they might follow variations within a jazz composition. We wanted the experience to feel open and exploratory, reflecting the spirit of Joans’ own work. blocks.text: The fact that Joans kept in touch with people like Langston Hughes, André Breton and Charlie Parker, yet never identified himself with any one artistic movement, leads you to what conclusion regarding his place within Surrealism, the Beat Generation and in the broader context of modern art?

What makes Joans so interesting is precisely that he never fit neatly into any category. He was close to Surrealism, in constant dialogue with Beat writers, and deeply immersed in jazz culture, yet he remained fiercely independent throughout his life. Rather than belonging to a single movement, he bridged several artistic worlds. I think his work encourages us to rethink the hierarchies that have shaped art history and to recognise the many connections between artistic practices, political movements, and cultural communities that have been too often considered separately. Once we stop viewing these movements in isolation, people and events often regarded as secondary begin to assume much greater importance. Joans emerges not on the margins of these histories but at their point of convergence, helping us see a far richer and more interconnected picture of twentieth-century culture. blocks.text: Collaboration and collective creativity were fundamental to Joans’ practice, especially through projects like Long Distance , which brought together 132 contributors over nearly three decades. What do these collaborative works reveal about his understanding of artistic authorship, community, and creative exchange?

Long Distance is a remarkable example of how Joans understood art as a collective endeavour. Over nearly thirty years, he invited artists, writers, musicians, and friends from around the world to contribute to a single work. The project reflects his openness to encounter and exchange, while never obscuring his own role as its instigator and guiding force. Rather than challenging authorship itself, Long Distance expands it into a space of dialogue and collaboration. These projects show how deeply he valued friendship, exchange, and the unexpected possibilities that emerge when people create together.

Joans described the merging of his artistic practice and lived experience as his Poem-Life. How did this philosophy shape your approach to presenting his personal archives, films, correspondence and artworks, and what questions did it raise about the relationship between an artist’s life and work?

The idea of a ” Poem-Life ” is central to understanding Joans. He didn’t separate art from everyday experience; travel, friendship, and conversation were all part of the creative process. At the same time, he had a remarkable awareness that these experiences mattered and should be documented. He was constantly encouraging people to ‘take a picture’, and throughout his life he carefully preserved photographs, letters, manuscripts, recordings, and ephemera. That is why we chose to present archival documents, correspondence, notebooks, films, and artworks together. Rather than treating the archive as background information, we approached it as an essential part of the work itself. The exhibition invites visitors to consider how closely artistic creation can be intertwined with the way a person lives, and how consciously Joans shaped the record of that life, occasionally blurring the line between documentation and self-mythology. blocks.text: Joans’ engagement with Pan-Africanism, Black Power, and international Surrealism offers perspectives on histories often presented separately. How might ‘Black Flower’ help reconsider established narratives of modern art, particularly the place of African and diasporic artists in its development?

We can no longer overlook the central role African and diasporic artists played in twentieth-century art. Many colleagues are working to bring these contributions into fuller view and to reconsider narratives that have too often kept these histories apart. Black Flower contributes to this work through Joan’s trajectory, showing how Black internationalism, Surrealism, jazz culture, and anti-colonial movements informed one another. Following his life and work helps us understand the postwar cultural landscape as a web of exchanges, reflecting the complexity of a postcolonial world in the making.
This exhibition is on view at the Musée Cantonal des Beaux-Arts in Lausanne until 28 February 2027.
